summary: CODEC combines Integrated Gradients-style contribution attribution with sparse autoencoders to decompose hidden-neuron contributions into sparse 'modes', applied to ResNet-50, a retinal CNN, and briefly ViT-B. The framework is conceptually appealing and the parallel treatment of biological and artificial networks is a genuine strength, but the empirical support has important gaps: baselines are essentially limited to activation-based SAEs, there are no seeds/error bars/significance tests on the headline claims, and the causal-control results are demonstrated on a very small number of qualitative examples with a single perturbation strategy. Novelty is moderate — SAEs on internal signals are now a well-developed literature that the paper positions only lightly against — and several core claims (sparsity/dimensionality/decorrelation trends across depth; superior controllability of contribution modes) would need proper statistical treatment and stronger interpretability baselines to be conference-ready.
strengths: Clear, well-motivated conceptual move from analyzing activations (receptive-field side) to analyzing contributions (composition of receptive and projective fields), which is a principled response to a known limitation of activation-based interpretability.

The framework is applied consistently across three settings (image CNN, retinal CNN model, Vision Transformer), and the retinal application is a distinctive contribution that shows biological interpretability yielding testable hypotheses (dynamic IRFs, error-correcting modes).

Combines four operations — attribution to hidden units, sparse decomposition, causal ablation/preservation, and input-space visualization — into a coherent pipeline that could serve as a reusable interpretability tool.

Reasonable engineering documentation of the SAE (dictionary size, threshold, L1, learning rate, epochs, batch size, training time) and a robustness scan over hyperparameters that identifies boundary regimes where reconstruction breaks down.

key_concerns.issue: The only real interpretability baseline is 'the same SAE applied to activations'. Class-correlation, controllability, and visualization results are not compared to established alternatives such as TCAV/CAVs, neuron ablation via Shapley/leave-one-out, feature visualization/circuit analysis, or non-SAE decompositions (NMF, ICA, PCA on contributions). Without these, the paper cannot show that contribution-modes beat existing tools rather than just beating activation-SAEs.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Add at least two competitive baselines from the interpretability literature for each headline claim (class-selectivity in Fig. 5, controllability in Fig. 6), and one non-autoencoder decomposition of the same contribution matrix (e.g., sparse NMF) to isolate the value of the SAE specifically.

key_concerns.issue: No statistical treatment of the main quantitative claims. The layerwise sparsity/decorrelation/dimensionality curves (Fig. 3B–F), class-correlation histograms (Fig. 5), and controllability curves (Fig. 6D–E) are reported without seeds, error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Reported R² of 0.85/0.84 is a single number. The 'sharp increase in ablation efficacy between blocks 6 and 7' is a strong scientific claim with no test.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Rerun key analyses across ≥3 seeds and report mean ± SE; add significance tests (paired/permutation) for contributions-vs-activations comparisons and for the block-6/7 shift; report variance across ImageNet classes rather than only aggregated performance scores.

key_concerns.issue: Generality is over-claimed relative to evidence. Abstract and Conclusion promise a framework that works across hierarchical layers and architectures, but ViT results are relegated to text ('ablation performance was inferior … further exploration is needed'), analyses are limited to selected blocks of ResNet-50, and no scaling to modern architectures (LLMs, ConvNeXt, larger ViTs) is shown. This weakens 'general framework' claims.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Either (i) run CODEC on at least one additional CNN (e.g., ConvNeXt or a ViT with a resolved spatial reduction) with the full quantitative pipeline, or (ii) scope the claims down explicitly to 'CNNs on image classification and small retinal CNNs' throughout the abstract and introduction.

key_concerns.issue: The causal-control story (Fig. 6) is under-specified and possibly cherry-picked. A single class ('black widow') anchors the qualitative example; the aggregate score is 'area between target and off-target curves', but there is no comparison to a strong controllability baseline (e.g., ablating channels ranked by class-conditional gradient magnitude, or by directly selecting channels with highest contribution to that class ignoring the SAE), so it is unclear whether the mode-selection is what buys the effect or just the contribution ranking.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Add a 'contribution-magnitude-only' baseline (top-k channels by class-conditional contribution, no SAE) and an activation-magnitude baseline, report results averaged over all 1000 classes with variance, and include a random-channel control matched in count.

key_concerns.issue: Related work is thin and does not engage with the very close prior literature on sparse dictionary decomposition of internal signals (SAE-based mechanistic interpretability, feature circuits, distributed alignment search, attribution-patching, activation patching, causal scrubbing). Contribution-based analyses of hidden units are cited essentially only through the Tanaka/Maheswaranathan retina line. Positioning is therefore not fair or complete.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Add a dedicated related-work section that contrasts CODEC with (a) SAEs on activations and residual streams, (b) attribution-patching and activation-patching, (c) direct logit attribution/attribution decomposition, and (d) causal-mediation-style analyses; and explain precisely what CODEC adds beyond each.

key_concerns.issue: Choice of Integrated Gradients to the top logit is under-motivated as the 'contribution target'. The paper notes 'top-1 was sufficient for reconstruction' but does not report how modes/downstream conclusions change under top-k or entropy targets, which are advertised as options.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Provide a supplementary sensitivity analysis showing that layerwise trends and mode–class correlations are qualitatively stable across at least two contribution targets and two attribution methods (IG vs. ActGrad vs. SmoothGrad).

key_concerns.issue: Interpretability claims in Fig. 7 ('shiny wood', 'hands', etc.) are anecdotal. There is no user study, no quantitative alignment with an interpretable concept set, and no test that the same mode fires on independent images sharing that concept.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Report a quantitative concept-alignment score (e.g., IoU with segmentation masks for a labeled attribute dataset such as CUB or Broden) for the visualized modes, or a small blinded human-rating study.

key_concerns.issue: The Limitations section is a single short paragraph and does not discuss failure modes surfaced within the paper itself (weaker ViT controllability, dependence on choice of target, hyperparameter boundary regimes, unclear behavior with residual/skip pathways).
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Expand Limitations to explicitly enumerate these, plus threats to validity of the biological interpretation (identifiability of modes, sensitivity to model fit quality of the retinal CNN).

questions_for_authors: How does CODEC compare quantitatively to SAEs trained on activations of the same layers when both are evaluated on the same downstream tasks (class prediction from loadings, causal ablation)? Fig. 5 shows a difference in class-correlation, but is that gap significant across seeds and layers?

For controllability (Fig. 6), how does the mode-based selection compare against a baseline that simply picks the top-k channels by their class-conditional contribution magnitude (no SAE)? Is the SAE providing the causal leverage, or is the underlying contribution ranking?

The layerwise decorrelation of positive and negative contributions is a striking claim. Is it robust to (a) other attribution methods, (b) subclasses of channels (e.g., channels with skip connections), and (c) tests against a null distribution generated by shuffling images within a channel?

How stable are the identified modes across seeds and across different SAE expansion factors? A stability score (e.g., matched-mode cosine similarity across runs) would make 'contribution modes' a more credible unit of analysis.
Why is the 3-layer retinal CNN's population 'surprisal' the right causal target, and how sensitive are the retinal findings (clusters, dynamic IRFs) to that choice vs. per-cell logit contribution?
For ViTs, what specific failure mode causes controllability to be 'inferior'? Is it the spatial-reduction choice, the residual-stream structure, or genuine over-distribution of computation?
calibration_check: The abstract and conclusion pitch CODEC as a general framework across biological and artificial networks, but the evidence base is one image CNN, one small retinal CNN, and a truncated ViT experiment without full quantitative results — the framing is somewhat broader than the experiments support.

significance.justification: Interpretability that bridges biological and artificial networks is a topic of active ICLR interest, and the retinal application is a genuine differentiator; but headline claims about mechanistic insight are largely descriptive and not yet clearly actionable for downstream researchers.

novelty.justification: Applying an SAE to Integrated-Gradients contributions rather than activations is a sensible but incremental twist on a well-established SAE-for-interpretability line; the retinal instantiation and mode-based control add some originality but do not by themselves constitute a strongly new mechanism.

rigor.justification: The method is internally coherent and the pipeline is described clearly, but many causal/control claims rest on selected examples and single-target attribution, without systematic controls that isolate whether the SAE, the contribution signal, or the ranking heuristic is doing the work.

statistical_soundness.justification: Almost no seeds, error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests on layerwise curves, class-correlation histograms, or controllability metrics; R² is reported as a single average across layers; the block-6/7 shift is asserted without a test.

calibration_honesty.justification: The paper hedges appropriately on ViTs and acknowledges some scope limits, but the abstract/conclusion still frame CODEC as a general biological-and-artificial framework beyond what the experiments show, and the Limitations section is unusually short.

clarity.justification: The prose is readable and the CODEC pipeline (target → algorithm → decomposition → visualization) is well organized; some equations (contribution mapping, IRF derivation) are compressed and the extraction artifacts do not obscure the logical structure.

structure_compliance.justification: Standard sections are present in a reasonable order (introduction, related tools, method, CNN experiments, control, visualization, biological application, ViT, conclusion, limitations) and within ICLR length norms; related-work coverage as a distinct section is thin.

reproducibility.justification: SAE hyperparameters, training regime, expansion factor, thresholds, and hardware/time are reported, and datasets (ImageNet val, a published retinal CNN) are standard; however, attribution choices, seed counts, evaluation protocols for controllability, and mode-matching procedures across layers are under-specified independently of any redacted code link.

related_work.justification: Positioning against the closest neighbors — SAEs for mechanistic interpretability, attribution/activation patching, circuit analysis, direct logit attribution, causal mediation — is largely absent, so it is hard to see what CODEC adds beyond the retina-CNN interpretability line it cites.

figure_quality.justification: Judging from captions, the display items are well-scoped to specific claims (contribution vs. activation matrices, sparsity/dimensionality curves, class-correlation histograms, ablation curves, dynamic IRFs), and the pipeline schematics look informative and pedagogically useful.

breadth_generality.justification: Coverage is one image CNN with selected blocks, one small retinal CNN, and a truncated ViT — this does not support the 'general framework across hierarchical layers and architectures' framing without additional models, datasets, or a scoped-down claim.

overall_recommendation.justification: A promising conceptual contribution and an unusually broad biological/artificial application, held back by missing baselines, missing statistics, and over-general framing; borderline reject in current form but plausibly acceptable after a major revision.
